claim: The boot command line ends with memtest=8
evidence: /proc/cmdline on this machine

claim: memtest= makes the kernel test memory early in boot and reserve bad regions
evidence: 'Memtest fills the memory with this pattern, validates memory contents and reserves bad memory regions that are detected.'

claim: The test writes a pattern to every free 64-bit word, reads it back and compares
evidence: memtest() loops over u64 words with WRITE_ONCE then READ_ONCE; do_one_pass() uses for_each_free_mem_range

claim: With memtest=8 the eight patterns are 0x88.., 0x44.., 0x22.., 0x11.., 0xaa.., 0x55.., 0xff.., 0x00.. in that order
evidence: early_memtest() runs i = 7 down to 0 over patterns[] = {0, ff.., 55.., aa.., 11.., 22.., 44.., 88.., ...}

claim: The final all-zero pass leaves memory zeroed
evidence: Source comment: 'The first entry has to be 0 to leave memtest with zeroed memory'

claim: On a mismatch the kernel prints the line and calls memblock_reserve on the range
evidence: reserve_bad_mem(): pr_info(...) then memblock_reserve(start_bad, end_bad - start_bad)

claim: A log line gives the pattern, the first bad byte and one past the last; the example range is 8 bytes
evidence: 0x1f4bb8800 - 0x1f4bb87f8 = 8; reserve_bad_mem is called with last_bad + incr where incr = sizeof(u64)

claim: There are 17 patterns and the last reads 'LINUXrlz' in little-endian byte order
evidence: patterns[] has 17 entries; struct.pack('<Q', 0x7a6c7258554e494c) = b'LINUXrlz'

claim: Only complete pages are released to the allocator; a page containing a reserved word is never released
evidence: __free_memory_core(): start_pfn = PFN_UP(start); end_pfn = PFN_DOWN(end); pages freed only for start_pfn < end_pfn

claim: All faulty cells sit in four neighbouring pages: 16 KiB of 16 GiB, one part in a million
